docs.title: Version Update Policy
docs.text:
• Terraform providers: Pin to minor version (~> X.Y). Review changelogs before major bumps.
  • Docker images: Pin to specific patch version. Avoid latest, stable, or major-only tags.
  • Packer base images: Use latest LTS cloud images. Rebuild templates after OS updates.
  • Samba AD DC: Uses latest tag (no version tags available). Consider pinning to digest for reproducibility.

docs.title: Updating Versions
docs.text:
1. Update the version in the relevant template or providers.tf
  2. For Terraform providers: delete .terraform.lock.hcl and run terraform init -upgrade
  3. For Docker images: the new image pulls automatically on next Nomad job deploy
  4. For PostgreSQL major version upgrades: requires pg_dump / pg_restore migration
  5. Test in a non-production environment before applying to the lab

docs.title: Setup Menu Reference
docs.text: The setup.sh script provides an interactive menu for all deployment and management operations.

docs.title: Running the Menu
docs.text:
./setup.sh          # Standard menu
./setup.sh --dev    # Standard menu + developer tools

docs.title: 1) Deploy all services
docs.text:
Runs the complete deployment from scratch:

  • Phase 1: Bootstrap (reads bootstrap.yml, creates API credentials, generates terraform.tfvars)
  • Phase 2: Packer template builds (skipped if templates 9001, 9002 already exist)
  • Phase 3: Layer 1 Terraform (Nomad cluster, Vault job)
  • Phase 4: Vault initialization
  • Phase 5: Layer 2 Terraform (PKI, secrets, Traefik, DNS, Authentik)

Total time: 20-40 minutes on first run.

docs.title: 2) Enable HA (keepalived VIPs)
docs.text:
Reads HA settings from bootstrap.yml and applies them: - Updates terraform/terraform.tfvars with HA variables - Applies Layer 1 Terraform (configures keepalived on all nodes) - Updates terraform/services/terraform.tfvars with VIP addresses - Applies Layer 2 Terraform (updates DNS records to point to VIPs)

Requires ha_dns_enabled or ha_traefik_enabled to be set in bootstrap.yml.

docs.title: 3) Kasm Workspaces
docs.text:
Deploys a Kasm Workspaces VM (VMID 930). Requires the Docker template (9001) to exist.

Equivalent to: 

docker compose run terraform apply -auto-approve -var "deploy_kasm=true"

docs.title: 4) Samba AD + LDAP Account Manager
docs.text:
Deploys Samba AD domain controllers and the LDAP Account Manager web UI. Sets up service accounts and Pi-hole DNS forwarding for the AD realm.

Uses enableService samba_ad and enableService lam.

docs.title: 5) Uptime Kuma (monitoring)
docs.text: Deploys Uptime Kuma service monitoring. Creates a status.<dns-suffix> DNS record.

docs.title: 6) Netbox (inventory management)
docs.text:
Deploys Netbox and auto-populates it with infrastructure inventory (VMs, LXC containers, Proxmox nodes, UniFi devices if configured).

Two-phase deployment: 1. Netbox job starts and database initializes 2. configure_netbox = true triggers inventory population via REST API

docs.title: 7) Rollback services (Layer 2)
docs.text:
Destroys all Layer 2 service resources while preserving infrastructure:

  • Stops Nomad jobs (Traefik, Authentik, Samba AD, etc.)
  • Destroys Vault PKI configuration, JWT auth, policies, secrets
  • Removes DNS records from Pi-hole
  • Removes Authentik apps and providers
  • Resets DNS on Nomad VMs and Proxmox nodes to gateway

Infrastructure (Nomad VMs, Pi-hole LXCs, Kasm) remains intact. After rollback, re-deploy services via option 1 starting from Phase 4, or use d5 from the developer menu.

Confirmation required: y/N

docs.title: 8) Rollback infrastructure (Layer 1 + 2)
docs.text:
Destroys all VMs and LXC containers. Also destroys Layer 2 resources first for clean shutdown.

Data loss

GlusterFS data lives on VM disks. Destroying VMs wipes all service data (Vault secrets, Authentik database, Samba AD, etc.). There is no recovery from this without a backup.

Steps: 1. Layer 2 destroy (clean service shutdown) 2. Reset Proxmox DNS to gateway 3. Layer 1 destroy (all VMs and LXC containers) 4. Clean generated config files 5. Optionally remove Packer templates (9001, 9002)

Confirmation required: Type DESTROY

docs.title: 9) Purge entire deployment
docs.text:
Full reset to pre-install state. Removes: - All VMs and LXC containers (via direct Proxmox API) - Packer templates (9999, 9001, 9002) - Cloud-init snippets - hashicorp@pam API user and HashicorpBuild role - DNS configuration (reset to gateway) - All generated config files (terraform.tfvars, cluster-info.json, crypto/)

Use this to start completely fresh, or to clean up after a failed deployment that left resources in an inconsistent state.

Confirmation required: Multiple prompts

docs.title: 0 or q) Exit
docs.text: Exits the menu.

docs.title: Developer Menu (--dev flag)
docs.text: Run with ./setup.sh --dev to access additional options.

docs.title: d1) Rebuild base Ubuntu template
docs.text:
Rebuilds the Packer Ubuntu 24.04 base template (VMID 9999). All other Packer templates (Docker, Nomad) clone from this. Use after significant OS updates or to refresh the cloud-init vendor snippet.

packer build -only='base-ubuntu.*' .

docs.title: d2) Rebuild service templates
docs.text:
Rebuilds the Docker (9001) and Nomad (9002) templates from the current base Ubuntu template. Use when you need to update Nomad, Docker, or other software installed in the templates.

packer build -only='ubuntu-docker.*' -only='ubuntu-nomad.*' .

docs.title: d3) Reset Proxmox user/token/role
docs.text:
Deletes and recreates the hashicorp@pam API user, HashicorpBuild role, and API token. Use if the API credentials become invalid or permissions need to be reset.

Requires root SSH access to Proxmox (uses the root password from bootstrap.yml).

docs.title: d4) Deploy infrastructure (Nomad, Vault, DNS)
docs.text:
Applies the full Layer 1 Terraform. Deploys or updates all infrastructure: - Nomad cluster - Pi-hole DNS cluster - Vault Nomad job - Kasm (if deploy_kasm=true)

docker compose run terraform apply -auto-approve

docs.title: d5) Deploy services (Traefik, Authentik, secrets)
docs.text:
Applies the full Layer 2 Terraform. Requires Layer 2 to be initialized (i.e., Vault must be running and terraform/services/terraform.tfvars must exist).

docker compose run terraform-services apply -auto-approve

docs.title: d6) Deploy Nomad cluster only
docs.text: Applies Layer 1 Terraform targeting only the Nomad module. Useful for updating Nomad VM configuration without affecting DNS or other resources.

docs.title: d7) Deploy DNS only
docs.text: Applies Layer 1 Terraform targeting only the Pi-hole DNS module.

docs.title: d8) Deploy Vault only
docs.text: Applies Layer 1 Terraform targeting the Vault job and directories, then runs Vault initialization and unseal.

docs.title: d9) Deploy Traefik only
docs.text: Deploys or redeployes Traefik via enableService traefik. Also re-issues the wildcard TLS certificate from Vault PKI.

docs.title: d10) Deploy Authentik only
docs.text: Deploys or redeploys Authentik via enableService authentik. Runs the two-phase deploy (job start, then app configuration).

docs.title: d11) Rebuild DNS records
docs.text: Re-applies only the DNS record Terraform resources without touching other Layer 2 resources. Use after adding services or changing the DNS suffix.

docs.title: Configuration Change Detection
docs.text:
When the menu starts, it compares bootstrap.yml against the deployed state. If changes are detected (such as new HA settings), it shows an alert:

  Configuration changes detected in bootstrap.yml:
    - Enable DNS HA (VIP: 192.168.1.3/24)
    - Enable Traefik HA (VIP: 192.168.1.100/24)
    *) Apply configuration changes

Select * to apply the detected changes. This calls the same logic as option 2.

docs.title: Using Terraform Directly
docs.text:
You can also run Terraform directly via Docker Compose:

# Layer 1 (infrastructure)
docker compose run terraform init
docker compose run terraform plan
docker compose run terraform apply -auto-approve

# Layer 2 (services)
docker compose run terraform-services init
docker compose run terraform-services plan
docker compose run terraform-services apply -auto-approve

# Target a specific resource
docker compose run terraform-services apply -auto-approve \
  -target=nomad_job.authentik

docs.title: Using Nomad Directly
docs.text:
# List all jobs
docker compose run --rm nomad job status

# View job details
docker compose run --rm nomad job status vault

# View allocation logs
docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job vault

# Stop a job
docker compose run --rm nomad job stop -purge vault

# List registered services
docker compose run --rm nomad service list

Note: Update NOMAD_ADDR in compose.yml if your nomad01 IP differs from the default.

docs.title: Rollback and Purge
docs.text: This page describes the three levels of rollback available and what each one destroys.

docs.title: Layer 2 Rollback (Services Only)
docs.text:
Menu option: 7) Rollback services

Destroys all service configuration while keeping the infrastructure (VMs, LXC containers) intact.

docs.title: What is destroyed
docs.text:
• All Layer 2 Nomad jobs: Traefik, Authentik, Samba AD, Uptime Kuma, LAM, Netbox, backup, Tailscale
  • Vault PKI (root CA, intermediate CA)
  • Vault JWT auth backend and all roles
  • Vault policies
  • Vault KV secrets (all generated passwords)
  • DNS records from Pi-hole (service hostnames)
  • Authentik applications and providers
  • TLS certificates (Traefik wildcard, Vault listener)

docs.title: What survives
docs.text:
• Nomad cluster VMs (nomad01, nomad02, nomad03)
  • Pi-hole LXC containers (dns-01, dns-02, dns-03)
  • Kasm VM (if deployed)
  • GlusterFS volumes and data (but services that wrote to them are no longer running)

docs.title: After rollback
docs.text:
DNS on Nomad VMs and Proxmox nodes is reset to the gateway IP (since Pi-hole is no longer configured with the correct records).

To redeploy services: 

./setup.sh --dev
# d5) Deploy services (Traefik, Authentik, secrets)

Or re-run the full deployment starting from Phase 4: 

./setup.sh
# 1) Deploy all services
# (Phases 1-2 are skipped since templates and VMs exist)

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text: The rollback prompts for confirmation: Are you sure? [y/N]

docs.title: Layer 1 Rollback (Infrastructure + Services)
docs.text:
Menu option: 8) Rollback infrastructure

Destroys all VMs and LXC containers. Also runs a Layer 2 rollback first for a clean shutdown.

docs.title: What is destroyed
docs.text:
Everything from Layer 2 rollback, plus:

  • All Nomad VMs (nomad01, nomad02, nomad03)
  • All Pi-hole LXC containers (dns-01, dns-02, dns-03)
  • Kasm VM (if deployed)
  • GlusterFS data — all service data (Vault, Authentik DB, Samba AD, Netbox, etc.)
  • Generated config files: terraform/services/terraform.tfvars, hosts.json, crypto/vault-credentials.json

docs.title: What survives
docs.text:
• Proxmox nodes (obviously)
  • Packer templates (9999, 9001, 9002) — preserved by default, optionally removed
  • bootstrap.yml
  • terraform/terraform.tfvars (but the Vault token/addresses in it are invalid)

GlusterFS data is on VM disks

GlusterFS data lives on VM local disks, not on NFS or shared storage. Destroying the VMs permanently destroys all service data. If you need to preserve data, back it up before rollback: 

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "sudo tar -czf /tmp/vault-backup.tar.gz /srv/gluster/nomad-data/vault"
scp labadmin@nomad01:/tmp/vault-backup.tar.gz ./

docs.title: After rollback
docs.text:
To redeploy from scratch: 

./setup.sh
# 1) Deploy all services
# Phase 1 (templates) skipped if 9001/9002 exist
# Phase 2 (VMs) deploys fresh VMs
# Phase 3 (Vault) initializes fresh Vault

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text: Requires typing DESTROY (uppercase) to confirm.

docs.title: Full Purge
docs.text:
Menu option: 9) Purge entire deployment

Resets the entire Proxmox environment to pre-install state. Used when you want a clean start or when Terraform state is too inconsistent to use destroy.

docs.title: What is destroyed
docs.text:
Everything from Layer 1 rollback, plus:

  • Packer templates (VMIDs 9999, 9001, 9002)
  • Cloud-init snippets from Proxmox storage
  • hashicorp@pam Proxmox API user
  • HashicorpBuild Proxmox role
  • DNS configuration reset to gateway on all Proxmox nodes
  • terraform.tfvars, cluster-info.json, hosts.json
  • crypto/ directory (SSH keys, API credentials, Vault credentials)

docs.title: Purge method
docs.text:
Unlike rollback (which uses terraform destroy), purge uses direct Proxmox API and SSH calls: - qm destroy <vmid> for VMs - pct destroy <vmid> for LXC containers - Proxmox API calls to remove snippets and users

This is more robust than Terraform destroy because it works even when Terraform state is inconsistent or when resources were created outside Terraform.

docs.title: After purge
docs.text:
The project directory is restored to a near-pristine state (only bootstrap.yml and project code remain). Re-run from scratch:

./setup.sh
# 1) Deploy all services
# All phases run fresh

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text: Multiple confirmation prompts. Requires explicit confirmation at each stage.

docs.title: Manual Recovery Commands
docs.text: If automated rollback fails (e.g., Nomad is unreachable), use these manual commands:

docs.title: Stop Nomad jobs directly
docs.text:
ssh labadmin@nomad01 <<'EOF'
for job in traefik authentik samba-ad uptime-kuma lam netbox backup tailscale; do
  nomad job stop -purge $job 2>/dev/null || true
done
EOF

docs.title: Remove VMs via Proxmox API
docs.text:
# Via SSH to Proxmox node
ssh root@<proxmox-ip> "qm stop 905; qm destroy 905"
ssh root@<proxmox-ip> "qm stop 906; qm destroy 906"
# etc.

docs.title: Reset DNS on Proxmox nodes
docs.text: ssh root@<proxmox-ip> "pvesh set /nodes/<nodename>/dns -dns1 <gateway-ip>"

docs.title: Clean generated files
docs.text:
rm -f terraform/services/terraform.tfvars
rm -f terraform/services/terraform.tfstate
rm -f terraform/vault.auto.tfvars
rm -f cluster-info.json hosts.json
# Optionally remove crypto directory:
rm -rf crypto/

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues and their solutions.

docs.title: Vault sealed after restart
docs.text:
Vault seals itself when the process restarts. The setup script unseals automatically during deployment, but manual intervention is needed after unplanned restarts.

VAULT_ADDR=$(jq -r '.vault_address' crypto/vault-credentials.json)
UNSEAL_KEY=$(jq -r '.unseal_key' crypto/vault-credentials.json)

curl -sk -X PUT "$VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/unseal" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"key\": \"$UNSEAL_KEY\"}"

docs.title: Vault initialized but credentials file missing
docs.text:
This means a previous deployment crashed after Vault initialized but before credentials were saved. The script auto-recovers:

  1. Detects initialized-but-no-credentials state
  2. Stops and wipes Vault data
  3. Redeploys Vault job
  4. Re-initializes fresh

This is triggered automatically when you re-run option 1.

docs.title: Permission denied on Vault storage
docs.text:
Vault cannot write to GlusterFS. Ensure the container is privileged:

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "docker inspect \$(docker ps -q --filter name=vault) | jq '.[0].HostConfig.Privileged'"

Should return true. If not, the Nomad job definition is incorrect — check that privileged = true is in the task config.

docs.title: Vault not accessible after TLS redeploy
docs.text:
After Vault redeploys with TLS, it seals itself and needs unseal. Also, the Nomad nodes may not yet trust the internal CA:

# Unseal
VAULT_ADDR="https://<nomad01-ip>:8200"
UNSEAL_KEY=$(jq -r '.unseal_key' crypto/vault-credentials.json)
curl -sk -X PUT "$VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/unseal" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"key\": \"$UNSEAL_KEY\"}"

# Check CA trust on Nomad nodes
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "openssl s_client -connect <nomad01-ip>:8200 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify|OK'"

docs.title: 404 errors for a service
docs.text:
1. Verify the service is running: nomad job status <service>
  2. Check service is registered: nomad service list
  3. Check Traefik knows about the router: 
    curl http://<nomad01-ip>:8081/api/http/routers | jq '.[].rule' | grep <service>
  4. Verify traefik.enable=true is in the Nomad service tags

docs.title: TLS certificate expired or missing
docs.text:
Re-issue the wildcard certificate by redeploying Traefik:

./setup.sh --dev
# d9) Deploy Traefik only

Verify: 

echo | openssl s_client -connect <dns-suffix>:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

docs.title: Service discovered but returns 502
docs.text:
The Traefik backend cannot reach the upstream service. Check:

  1. Is the upstream service running? Check Nomad allocation logs
  2. Is the service listening on the correct port?
  3. For HTTPS backends (like Vault): ensure --serversTransport.insecureSkipVerify=true is in Traefik args

docs.title: FQDN not resolving but IP works
docs.text:
Your client is not using Pi-hole for DNS. Configure your device to use the Pi-hole IP (or HA VIP):

# Verify which DNS you're using
nslookup vault.<dns-suffix>
# Should show "Server: <pihole-ip>"

docs.title: DNS resolves to wrong IP
docs.text:
DNS records may be outdated. Rebuild them:

./setup.sh --dev
# d11) Rebuild DNS records

docs.title: Container provisioning fails during apt-get
docs.text:
Your network blocks external DNS. Set bootstrap_dns to your gateway:

# terraform/terraform.tfvars
bootstrap_dns = "<gateway-ip>"

Then re-run the deployment.

docs.title: Pi-hole not syncing between nodes
docs.text:
Test Gravity Sync connectivity:

ssh labadmin@dns-01 "ssh -i /etc/gravity-sync/gravity-sync.rsa dns-02 echo ok"

Run sync manually:

ssh labadmin@dns-01 "sudo gravity sync push"
ssh labadmin@dns-02 "sudo gravity sync logs"

docs.title: GlusterFS not mounted
docs.text:
The GlusterFS sentinel file check is failing. Run the mount fix:

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "mountpoint -q /srv/gluster/nomad-data && echo mounted || echo NOT MOUNTED"

# If not mounted, restart glusterd
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "sudo systemctl restart glusterd"
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "sudo mount -a"

Check the sentinel: 

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "ls -la /srv/gluster/nomad-data/.mount-sentinel"

If the sentinel is missing, create it: 

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "sudo touch /srv/gluster/nomad-data/.mount-sentinel"

docs.title: Nomad job stuck in pending
docs.text:
The job cannot be scheduled. Common causes:

# Check job status and why it's not scheduled
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "nomad job status <job>"
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "nomad alloc status <alloc-id>"

Common issues: - GlusterFS not mounted (prestart task failing) - Constraint not matching (e.g., hostname == nomad01 but node is nomad01.mylab.lan) - Resource constraints (not enough CPU/memory)

docs.title: Nomad cluster not forming quorum
docs.text:
Check that all three Nomad nodes can see each other:

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "nomad server members"

Should show all three nodes as alive. If a node shows as failed, check: 1. Is the Nomad service running? systemctl status nomad 2. Can nodes reach each other? ping nomad02 3. Are retry_join IPs correct in /etc/nomad.d/nomad.hcl?

docs.title: Authentik not starting
docs.text:
Check allocation logs:

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "nomad alloc logs -job authentik -task authentik-server"

Common causes: - Vault WIF authentication failing (check Vault is unsealed and accessible) - PostgreSQL not ready yet (Authentik starts before DB is fully initialized — wait 30-60s) - GlusterFS directories missing

docs.title: Admin password doesn't match Vault
docs.text:
The admin password is set during first database initialization. If Vault was reinitialized with different secrets:

# Get current password from Vault
ADMIN_PW=$(vault kv get -field=admin_password secret/authentik)
API_TOKEN=$(vault kv get -field=api_token secret/authentik)

# Get admin user PK
ADMIN_PK=$(curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
  "https://<nomad01-ip>:9443/api/v3/core/users/?username=akadmin" | jq -r '.results[0].pk')

# Reset password
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -X POST "https://<nomad01-ip>:9443/api/v3/core/users/$ADMIN_PK/set_password/" \
  -d "{\"password\":$(echo "$ADMIN_PW" | jq -Rs .)}"

docs.title: goauthentik Terraform provider errors
docs.text:
The goauthentik/authentik Terraform provider has known bugs with invalidation_flow on OAuth2 and LDAP providers. All Authentik configuration is done via REST API (null_resource + curl) for this reason. If you see provider errors, check if the API-based provisioning succeeded:

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api-token>' \
  https://<nomad01-ip>:9443/api/v3/core/applications/ | jq '[.results[].name]'"

docs.title: Domain controller not starting
docs.text:
# Check container status
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "docker ps | grep samba"
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "nomad alloc logs -job samba-ad"

Common causes: - GlusterFS not mounted for the samba data directories - Port 88/389/445 already in use (check for previous stale allocations) - DNS not resolving AD realm (verify Pi-hole has AD DNS forwarding)

docs.title: Replication between DC01 and DC02 failing
docs.text:
# Check replication status inside DC01
CONTAINER=$(docker ps --format '{{.ID}} {{.Names}}' | grep samba-ad | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')
docker exec $CONTAINER samba-tool drs showrepl

Check DNS connectivity between nodes: 

dig @<dns-01-ip> _ldap._tcp.<ad-realm-lowercase> SRV

docs.title: Domain join fails for a NAS
docs.text:
1. Verify DNS: dig @<dns-01-ip> <ad-realm-lowercase> should resolve
  2. Verify domain-join-svc account exists in AD: 
    docker exec $CONTAINER samba-tool user show domain-join-svc
  3. Check the join credentials are correct in Vault: 
    vault kv get secret/samba-ad/service-accounts

docs.title: VIP not bound on any node
docs.text:
# Check keepalived logs
ssh labadmin@dns-01 "journalctl -u keepalived -n 30"

Common issues: - VRRP router ID conflict with another device on the network - Firewall blocking VRRP multicast (protocol 112) - VRRP password mismatch (check it is identical on all nodes, max 8 chars)

docs.title: DNS still failing even with HA VIP
docs.text:
Check the VIP is bound and responding:

# Is VIP bound on any node?
ssh labadmin@dns-01 "ip addr show eth0 | grep <vip-ip>"
ssh labadmin@dns-02 "ip addr show eth0 | grep <vip-ip>"

# Does Pi-hole respond on the VIP?
dig @<vip-ip> google.com

docs.title: Build fails downloading cloud image
docs.text:
The base Ubuntu cloud image download may fail due to network issues:

# Check what's happening in Packer
docker compose run packer build -debug -only='base-ubuntu.*' .

If your network requires a proxy, set the appropriate environment variables before running Packer.

docs.title: Template already exists error
docs.text:
Packer may fail if a partial template from a previous failed build exists:

# Remove the partial template
ssh root@<proxmox-ip> "qm status 9999 && qm destroy 9999 || true"

Then retry the build.

docs.title: v2 Refactor (refactor/v2)
docs.text: Status doc for the "new version" of proxmox-lab — the refactor/v2 branch.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
refactor/v2 is the active development line and the intended successor to main. It is an IaC-first rewrite: work that used to live in lib/*.sh bash moved into Terraform / Packer / Nomad, and the storage layer moved from GlusterFS to CSI + NFS on TrueNAS. It is a net simplification — more code removed than added.

Metric Value Commits ahead of main 252 (2026-04-10 → 2026-09-02) Diff vs main 209 files, +17,634 / −22,195 (net −4,561 lines) lib/ (bash) change +2,395 / −8,427 (~6k lines of bash removed) Merge state ✅ Merged 2026-09-28 — main @ 1620c06, tagged v2.0.0, release/v2 cut (mirrors release/v1/v1.0.0)

Point-in-time source-control status (unpushed commits, stashes, deployed-vs-repo gaps on the admin host) is tracked in your site overlay's project-updates/ (see docs/getting-started/local-overlay.md), not here — that state changes as the branch is pushed/merged.

docs.title: What changed (major workstreams)
docs.text:
The refactor was executed as several phased arcs (commit subjects tagged "Phase N"):

  1. Storage: GlusterFS → CSI + NFS (May 27–28, Phases 0–3)
  2. Per-service TrueNAS datasets + NFS exports; deploy csi-driver-nfs plugin; Nomad jobs mount CSI volumes (multi-node-multi-writer).

  3. Stripped GlusterFS install + gluster-write code out of vm-nomad and the services layer. (GlusterFS is now decommissioned on the live lab; Vault uses Raft.)

  4. Vault HA (May 4, Phases 1–4)

  5. Single Vault → system job + integrated Raft cluster; listener cert covers every Nomad node; multi-node unseal flow; DNS-based Nomad WIF address.

  6. Roaming profiles (May 18, Phases 1–5)

  7. Extended nas_servers schema; auto-create TrueNAS dataset/share/ACL; profile-reconciler periodic Nomad job; d16 manual reconcile trigger.

  8. NAS classification + ACLs (June, Phases 4–5)

  9. validateNASStorage preflight gate in bootstrap; nas-acls + dataset/group model (ties into the ISO-27001 four-tier data classification).

  10. Bash → IaC / setup flow (throughout)

  11. Rewrote setup.sh around a bootstrap flow; removed sed-based config mutation; replaced the bash YAML parser with python3; SSH-based agent install → cloud-init vendor snippet; deleted dead bash deploy scripts, old Nomad job files, orphaned docs.

  12. Services added / reworked

  13. unifi-dns (Nomad job + Vault/OIDC/DNS wiring); netbox with a periodic UniFi sync job (replaced a one-shot scrape); Kasm SAML → LDAP outpost for credential passthrough; Uptime Kuma → 2.x; Authentik application/OIDC wiring.

  14. Networking / PKI / hardening

  15. Nomad VMs → static IPs; PKI chain EC → RSA (root/intermediate 4096, leaf 2048); apt sources → HTTPS (fixes deploys on networks blocking port 80); Layer 2 split around the DNS LXC deploy to break a circular dependency.

docs.title: How it was merged (2026-09-28)
docs.text:
main was fast-forwarded to refactor/v2 (main was 0 behind, so linear history — no merge commit), then tagged and branched to mirror the v1 release convention (release/v1 + v1.0.0):

# both Terraform roots validated first (whole-repo docker mount so ../../nomad resolves):
docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/sh -v "$(pwd):/repo" -w /repo/terraform          hashicorp/terraform:1.14 -c 'terraform init -backend=false >/dev/null 2>&1 && terraform validate'
docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/sh -v "$(pwd):/repo" -w /repo/terraform/services hashicorp/terraform:1.14 -c 'terraform init -backend=false >/dev/null 2>&1 && terraform validate'
# → both "Success! The configuration is valid."

git push origin refactor/v2:main            # ff main → 1620c06
git push origin refactor/v2:release/v2      # cut release/v2
git tag -a v2.0.0 refactor/v2 -m "…" && git push origin v2.0.0

release/v1 + v1.0.0 remain pinned, so v1 is preserved.

docs.title: Vault HA — 3-node integrated Raft cluster
docs.text: Status: Deferred. To be picked up on the next clean cluster rebuild. Branch: feature/vault-ha (this branch holds only the plan; implementation lands here when work begins). Date drafted: 2026-05-04 (during refactor/v2 deploy stabilization).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Today Vault is a single-instance Nomad job hard-pinned to nomad01, with file storage on GlusterFS, 1-of-1 Shamir unseal, Nomad's WIF integration pointing at nomad01's IP, and DNS routing through Traefik. If nomad01 (or its Vault container) goes down, every Vault-dependent service — Authentik, Samba AD, Netbox, the new Backup/Tailscale jobs — fails to fetch secrets and either alloc-fails or runs degraded.

The lab has 3 Nomad servers (nomad01-03) with shared GlusterFS, so the substrate to spread Vault across all of them is already in place. Goal: make Vault survive any one node going down without manual recovery.

docs.title: Why integrated Raft (not Consul / file / others)
docs.text:
• Built into Vault — no extra HA-storage cluster to operate.
  • Self-replicating; loses GlusterFS dependency for the Vault data path. (GlusterFS stays for everything else; Vault gets its own Raft replication.)
  • Native cluster awareness — request forwarding, snapshots, peer auto-join via retry_join.
  • Works with our existing Shamir unseal flow; no cloud KMS needed.

docs.title: Recommended end-state
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
                │       Traefik (HA via VIP)          │
                │     vault.mylab.lan → :8200         │
                └───────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                │ load-balances
       ┌────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
       ▼                        ▼                        ▼
  ┌──────────┐             ┌──────────┐             ┌──────────┐
  │ nomad01  │             │ nomad02  │             │ nomad03  │
  │ vault    │◀═══raft═══▶ │ vault    │◀═══raft═══▶ │ vault    │
  │ leader   │             │ follower │             │ follower │
  │ /data/   │             │ /data/   │             │ /data/   │
  │ vault    │             │ vault    │             │ vault    │
  │ (LOCAL)  │             │ (LOCAL)  │             │ (LOCAL)  │
  └──────────┘             └──────────┘             └──────────┘
  • 3-node Raft cluster, one Vault per Nomad node (type = "system" or 3-count service).
  • Storage moves from file on GlusterFS to raft on each VM's local /var/lib/vault (or a per-node subdir under GlusterFS — both work, local disk is simpler).
  • Shamir 1-of-3 (one key, threshold 1) keeps the existing operational model — operator unseals each node once after a cold start.
  • Nomad's vault {} stanza points at https://vault.mylab.lan:8200 (Traefik-fronted) so any single Vault going away doesn't matter.
  • Backup uses vault operator raft snapshot (consistent, atomic) instead of tar-of-file-storage.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and decisions
docs.text:
1. Auto-unseal vs. manual. Full automation needs a transit/KMS keypair somewhere durable. Recommendation: stay with Shamir manual-unseal, but extend unsealVault.sh to walk all 3 nodes. Cold start = 3 unseal calls, but no extra infra.
  2. Migration vs. greenfield. Two paths:
  3. a) Snapshot existing single-node Vault → deploy 3-node Raft → restore → re-init dynamic auth. ~30 min downtime; preserves all current secrets.
  4. b) Wait for next clean rebuild and bring up Raft from day one. Zero migration risk.

For a lab still under heavy churn, (b) is much safer. This branch assumes (b). 3. Local disk vs. GlusterFS for Raft data. Raft expects fast local fsync. GlusterFS works but adds latency and risks partial-write weirdness. Local disk per-node is the standard pattern. Operationally fine — Raft does the replication.

docs.title: Phase 1: Job template restructure
docs.text:
File: terraform/services/templates/vault.nomad.hcl.tpl (or keep in Layer 1 with a feature flag)

  • Drop constraint { value = "nomad01" }.
  • count = 3 (or type = "system").
  • Per-instance node_id from ${node.unique.name}.
  • Storage stanza: 
    storage "raft" {
  path    = "/data/vault"
  node_id = "${node.unique.name}"
  retry_join { leader_api_addr = "https://nomad01.${dns_postfix}:8200" }
  retry_join { leader_api_addr = "https://nomad02.${dns_postfix}:8200" }
  retry_join { leader_api_addr = "https://nomad03.${dns_postfix}:8200" }
}
  • api_addr / cluster_addr keep the {{ sockaddr ... }} template — already correct for HA.
  • Per-node bind-mount: either /srv/gluster/nomad-data/vault/${node.unique.name} (separate dirs on shared FS) or a non-gluster volume claim. Local disk preferred.

docs.title: Phase 2: Cert + DNS
docs.text:
Files: terraform/services/tls-certificates.tf, terraform/services/dns-records.tf

  • Add nomad02.${dns_postfix} / nomad03.${dns_postfix} + IPs to Vault listener cert SANs, OR reuse the existing *.${dns_postfix} wildcard cert (simpler).
  • DNS already routes vault.${dns_postfix} through Traefik; once count = 3, Nomad's service registry lists all instances and Traefik picks them up automatically.

docs.title: Phase 3: Init / unseal flow
docs.text:
Files: lib/deploy/nomadJob/initVault.sh, lib/deploy/nomadJob/unsealVault.sh, setup.sh

  • initAndUnsealVault: init runs once on the first booted node (auto-elects leader). Save key + token (unchanged). Then unseal each node in turn — 02 and 03 join via retry_join after they're unsealed.
  • unsealVault: iterate all Vault instances from Nomad's service catalog instead of single IP. Idempotent.
  • setup.sh Phase 3: wait for ALL 3 to report sealed=true, unseal each, verify all sealed=false.

docs.title: Phase 4: Nomad WIF
docs.text:
File: terraform/services/nomad-vault-integration.tf

  • Change vault_addr in each Nomad's /etc/nomad.d/vault.hcl from a hardcoded IP to https://vault.${dns_postfix}:8200 (Traefik-fronted). Internal CA still issues the listener cert, so the existing trust-store push is unchanged.

docs.title: Phase 5: Backup
docs.text:
File: terraform/services/templates/backup.nomad.hcl.tpl

  • Replace tar -czf vault.tar.gz /data/vault with vault operator raft snapshot save against https://vault.${dns_postfix}:8200, authed via WIF.
  • Document restore: vault operator raft snapshot restore against a freshly initialized Vault.

docs.title: Phase 6: Documentation
docs.text:
File: .claude/CLAUDE.md

  • Update Vault Configuration: 3-node Raft, manual Shamir across all nodes, Traefik-fronted DNS, raft-snapshot backups.
  • Operational note: cold-cluster start = 3 unseal calls.
  • Troubleshooting: "one Vault sealed, others fine" — forward unseal to the right node.

docs.title: Files Summary
docs.text: File Action Purpose terraform/services/templates/vault.nomad.hcl.tpl new (move from Layer 1) Raft, count=3, retry_join terraform/templates/vault.nomad.hcl.tpl deprecate or feature-flag Keep single-node bootstrap path optional terraform/services/tls-certificates.tf modify SANs for all 3 nodes terraform/services/nomad-vault-integration.tf modify vault_addr → DNS lib/deploy/nomadJob/initVault.sh modify Unseal all 3 after init lib/deploy/nomadJob/unsealVault.sh modify Walk all instances setup.sh (Phase 3 of deployAll) modify Wait+unseal all 3, verify all open terraform/services/templates/backup.nomad.hcl.tpl modify Raft snapshot vs. tar .claude/CLAUDE.md modify Doc the new model

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
1. nomad job status vault shows 3 running allocs across nomad01/02/03.
  2. vault operator raft list-peers shows 3 voters, one leader.
  3. Stop nomad01's Vault alloc; Authentik/Samba/Netbox keep working — Traefik routes to a survivor.
  4. After full cluster reboot: unsealVault.sh opens all 3, vault status shows sealed=false everywhere.
  5. vault operator raft snapshot save /tmp/test.snap produces a non-empty file.
  6. Backup job logs show snapshot creation; snapshot lands in NFS/SMB target.

docs.title: Picking this up
docs.text:
When ready to implement:

git checkout feature/vault-ha
git rebase main          # or refactor/v2 if v2 hasn't merged yet
# implement against this plan

Coordinate with: next clean cluster rebuild (greenfield path 2b above).

docs.title: Authentik
docs.text: Authentik is a self-hosted identity provider that provides single sign-on (SSO) for lab services. It supports OAuth2, OpenID Connect (OIDC), SAML, and LDAP protocols.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Property Value Nomad Job authentik Type service (count 1) Node Pinned to nomad01 Vault Role authentik (WIF) Ports 9000 (HTTP), 9443 (HTTPS), 5432 (PostgreSQL) Network Mode Host Storage /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/ (GlusterFS) Version 2026.2+ (Redis removed in 2025.10 — PostgreSQL handles caching)

docs.title: Task Resource Allocation
docs.text: Task Image CPU Memory PostgreSQL postgres:16-alpine 200 MHz 512 MB Server ghcr.io/goauthentik/server:2026.x 500 MHz 1024 MB Worker ghcr.io/goauthentik/server:2026.x 300 MHz 512 MB

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Authentik is deployed as part of the core stack (option 1). It is also deployed automatically during the first run. To deploy or redeploy independently:

./setup.sh
# Select option 9: Deploy Authentik

Or deploy directly with the Nomad CLI:

docker compose run --rm nomad job run /nomad/jobs/authentik.nomad.hcl

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before deploying Authentik, all of the following must be in place:

  1. Nomad cluster -- All three Nomad nodes operational
  2. Traefik -- Reverse proxy running (menu option 7)
  3. Vault -- Secrets manager running and initialized (menu option 8)
  4. Vault secrets -- Authentik secrets stored at secret/data/authentik:
    • secret_key -- Authentik's internal signing key
    • postgres_password -- PostgreSQL database password
  5. Pi-hole DNS -- auth.<dns_postfix> resolving to nomad01
  6. GlusterFS -- Shared volume mounted at /srv/gluster/nomad-data

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph clients["Clients"]
        BROWSER[Browser]
    end

    subgraph nomad01["nomad01"]
        TRAEFIK[Traefik<br/>:443]

        subgraph authentik_group["Authentik Nomad Group"]

            REDIS[Redis<br/>:6379<br/>prestart sidecar]

    end

    REDIS --> REDIS_DATA

docs.title: Multi-Task Architecture
docs.text: Authentik runs as four tasks within a single Nomad group. This ensures all components are co-located on the same node and share the same network namespace.

docs.title: Task Lifecycle
docs.text:
graph LR
    PG[PostgreSQL<br/>prestart sidecar] --> SERVER[Authentik Server<br/>main task]
    REDIS[Redis<br/>prestart sidecar] --> SERVER
    PG --> WORKER[Authentik Worker<br/>main task]
    REDIS --> WORKER

PostgreSQL and Redis are configured as prestart sidecars (lifecycle { hook = "prestart"; sidecar = true }). This means:

  • They start before the main tasks (Server and Worker)
  • They continue running for the lifetime of the group
  • If they fail, the entire group is restarted

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
PostgreSQL provides the primary data store for Authentik.

Property Value Image postgres:16-alpine Port 5432 User root (container user) Database authentik DB User authentik Storage /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/postgres

The database password is injected from Vault via a template:

template {
  data = <<EOH
POSTGRES_USER=authentik
POSTGRES_DB=authentik
{{ with secret "secret/data/authentik" }}
POSTGRES_PASSWORD={{ .Data.data.postgres_password }}
{{ end }}
PGDATA=/var/lib/postgresql/data
EOH
  destination = "secrets/postgres.env"
  env         = true
}

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
Redis serves as the cache and message broker for Authentik's background task system.

Property Value Image redis:7-alpine Port 6379 Persistence RDB snapshot every 60 seconds if at least 1 key changed Storage /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/redis

docs.title: Authentik Server
docs.text:
The server task handles the web UI, API endpoints, and authentication flows.

Property Value Image ghcr.io/goauthentik/server:2025.12 Args ["server"] HTTP Port 9000 HTTPS Port 9443 Storage authentik/media, authentik/templates

docs.title: Authentik Worker
docs.text:
The worker task handles background processing such as email sending, LDAP sync, and scheduled tasks.

Property Value Image ghcr.io/goauthentik/server:2025.12 Args ["worker"] Storage authentik/media, authentik/certs

The worker has no service registration or health check since it does not serve HTTP traffic.

docs.title: Vault Secret Injection
docs.text:
Authentik uses Nomad's Vault integration with Workload Identity Federation to fetch secrets at runtime. The group-level vault stanza configures this:

vault {
  role        = "authentik"
  change_mode = "restart"
}
  • role = "authentik" -- Nomad presents a JWT to Vault's jwt-nomad auth backend with this role, which maps to the authentik Vault policy.
  • change_mode = "restart" -- If the secrets at secret/data/authentik change, all tasks in the group are restarted to pick up the new values.

docs.title: Secrets Retrieved
docs.text:
Both the Server and Worker tasks use identical template blocks to inject secrets as environment variables:

Environment Variable Vault Path Key AUTHENTIK_SECRET_KEY secret/data/authentik secret_key AUTHENTIK_POSTGRESQL__PASSWORD secret/data/authentik postgres_password

The template block:

template {
  data = <<EOH
{{ with secret "secret/data/authentik" }}
AUTHENTIK_SECRET_KEY={{ .Data.data.secret_key }}
AUTHENTIK_POSTGRESQL__PASSWORD={{ .Data.data.postgres_password }}
{{ end }}
AUTHENTIK_POSTGRESQL__HOST=127.0.0.1
AUTHENTIK_POSTGRESQL__PORT=5432
AUTHENTIK_POSTGRESQL__USER=authentik
AUTHENTIK_POSTGRESQL__NAME=authentik
AUTHENTIK_REDIS__HOST=127.0.0.1
AUTHENTIK_REDIS__PORT=6379
AUTHENTIK_ERROR_REPORTING__ENABLED=false
EOH
  destination = "secrets/authentik.env"
  env         = true
}

Since all tasks run in host networking mode on the same node, PostgreSQL and Redis are reached at 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Traefik Integration
docs.text:
Authentik registers with Traefik for HTTP and HTTPS routing:

tags = [
  "traefik.enable=true",
  "traefik.http.routers.authentik-http.rule=Host(`auth.<domain>`) || Host(`auth`)",
  "traefik.http.routers.authentik-http.entrypoints=web",
  "traefik.http.routers.authentik.rule=Host(`auth.<domain>`) || Host(`auth`)",
  "traefik.http.routers.authentik.entrypoints=websecure",
  "traefik.http.routers.authentik.tls=true",
  "traefik.http.routers.authentik.tls.certresolver=step-ca",
  "traefik.http.services.authentik.loadbalancer.server.port=9000",
]

Access Authentik at:

  • https://auth.<dns_postfix> (HTTPS via Traefik)
  • http://nomad01:9000 (direct, no TLS)

docs.title: Health Check
docs.text:
The Authentik Server task registers a health check with Nomad:

check {
  type     = "http"
  path     = "/-/health/live/"
  port     = "http"
  interval = "30s"
  timeout  = "5s"
}

The /-/health/live/ endpoint returns 200 when the Authentik server is accepting requests.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text: After the first deployment, Authentik requires an initial setup to create the default admin account.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open https://auth.<dns_postfix>/if/flow/initial-setup/ in a browser.
  2. Create the initial admin account (default username is akadmin).
  3. Set a strong password for the admin account.
  4. Log in to the Authentik admin interface.

First-Time Only

The initial setup flow is only available when no admin account exists. If you need to reset the admin account, you must access the PostgreSQL database directly.

docs.title: Accessing the Admin Interface
docs.text:
After initial setup, the admin interface is available at:

https://auth.<dns_postfix>/if/admin/

docs.title: SSO Capabilities
docs.text:
Authentik supports multiple authentication protocols for integrating with lab services:

Protocol Use Case OAuth2 / OIDC Modern web applications, API authentication SAML Enterprise applications, legacy systems LDAP Applications requiring directory-style authentication Proxy Forward authentication for services behind Traefik

docs.title: Common Integrations
docs.text:
Authentik can provide SSO for:

  • Proxmox VE (OIDC)
  • Nomad UI (OIDC)
  • Vault UI (OIDC)
  • Grafana (OAuth2)
  • Any Traefik-proxied service (Forward Auth)

docs.title: Storage Paths
docs.text:
All Authentik data is stored on GlusterFS:

Path Contents /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/postgres PostgreSQL database files /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/redis Redis RDB snapshots /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/media Uploaded media (icons, backgrounds) /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/templates Custom email/page templates /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/certs Certificates used by the worker

docs.title: Verifying the Deployment
docs.text:
After deploying Authentik, verify all components are running:

# Check job status (all 4 tasks should be running)
docker compose run --rm nomad job status authentik

# Check allocation health
docker compose run --rm nomad alloc status -job authentik

# Check the health endpoint
curl -s http://nomad01:9000/-/health/live/

# Verify the service is registered in Nomad
docker compose run --rm nomad service list

# Check Traefik has discovered Authentik
curl -s http://nomad01:8081/api/http/routers | jq '.[] | select(.name | contains("authentik"))'

# View allocation logs for a specific task
docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job authentik server
docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job authentik postgres

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Authentik Server not starting

The server task fails to start or restarts repeatedly.

  1. Check the server task logs: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job authentik server
  2. Verify PostgreSQL is running: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job authentik postgres
  3. Verify Redis is running: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job authentik redis
  4. Check that Vault secrets are accessible: 
    export VAULT_ADDR="http://nomad01:8200"
vault kv get secret/authentik
Vault secrets not being injected

Authentik tasks fail because secrets are missing.

  1. Verify the Vault role exists: 
    export VAULT_ADDR="http://nomad01:8200"
vault read auth/jwt-nomad/role/authentik
  2. Verify the secrets exist in Vault: 
    vault kv get secret/authentik
  3. Check that Vault is unsealed: 
    curl -s http://nomad01:8200/v1/sys/seal-status | jq .sealed
  4. Inspect the Nomad job events for Vault errors: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad job status authentik
Database connection errors

Authentik cannot connect to PostgreSQL.

  1. Verify PostgreSQL is running and healthy: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job authentik postgres
  2. Test the database connection from nomad01: 
    ssh nomad01 'docker exec $(docker ps -qf name=postgres) pg_isready'
  3. Check that the PostgreSQL data directory has correct permissions: 
    ssh nomad01 'ls -la /srv/gluster/nomad-data/authentik/postgres'
Initial setup page not loading

The /if/flow/initial-setup/ page returns an error or redirect loop.

  1. Verify Authentik is healthy: 
    curl -s http://nomad01:9000/-/health/live/
  2. Check that you are using the correct URL (trailing slash matters): 
    https://auth.<dns_postfix>/if/flow/initial-setup/
  3. If an admin account already exists, use the regular login page: 
    https://auth.<dns_postfix>/if/flow/default-authentication-flow/

docs.title: Kasm Workspaces
docs.text: Kasm Workspaces provides browser-based remote desktops and application streaming. It is deployed as an optional Proxmox VM (VMID 930).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Property Value Type Proxmox VM VMID 930 Template ubuntu-docker (9001) Module terraform/vm-kasm/ Ports 443 (HTTPS web UI) Credentials Admin password from Vault at secret/kasm

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Select option 3 from the setup menu:

./setup.sh
# 3) Kasm Workspaces

Or apply directly via Layer 1 Terraform:

docker compose run terraform apply -auto-approve -var "deploy_kasm=true"

Prerequisites

Vault and Traefik must be deployed before Kasm. The Kasm admin password is read from Vault at deploy time (secret/kasm -> admin_password).

docs.title: Accessing Kasm
docs.text:
After deployment, Kasm is accessible at:

https://<kasm-ip>  (direct, self-signed Kasm cert)

DNS record (kasm.<dns-suffix>) points directly to the Kasm VM IP, not through Traefik. Kasm handles its own TLS.

Default admin credentials: - URL: https://<kasm-ip> - Username: admin@kasm.local - Password: From Vault: vault kv get -field=admin_password secret/kasm

docs.title: LDAP Authentication with Samba AD
docs.text: To configure Kasm to authenticate via Samba AD LDAP, see the tutorial: Kasm LDAP Authentication.

docs.title: Cloud-init Provisioning
docs.text: The Kasm VM is provisioned via cloud-init (terraform/vm-kasm/cloudinit/kasm-user-data.tmpl). The cloud-init script: 1. Sets hostname and SSH authorized key 2. Installs Kasm Workspaces (downloads installer, runs kasm_installer.sh) 3. Sets the admin password

docs.title: Kasm installer fails
docs.text:
The Kasm installer downloads a large package from the internet. Ensure the VM has internet access and DNS is working:

ssh labadmin@kasm01 "curl -v https://kasm.io"

docs.title: Admin login fails
docs.text:
Retrieve the password from Vault:

vault kv get -field=admin_password secret/kasm

If the password is incorrect (e.g., redeployed with different Vault data), reset it via Kasm's CLI:

ssh labadmin@kasm01 "sudo /opt/kasm/bin/utils/api_server_mgmt.py --reset-admin-password"

docs.title: Netbox
docs.text: Netbox is an infrastructure inventory and documentation tool. When deployed, it is automatically populated with your lab's VMs, LXC containers, Proxmox physical nodes, and optionally UniFi network devices.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Property Value Nomad Job netbox Node Pinned to nomad01 Port 8080 (HTTP) Vault Role netbox (WIF) Storage /srv/gluster/nomad-data/netbox/ (GlusterFS) Secrets secret/netbox in Vault

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Select option 6 from the setup menu:

./setup.sh
# 6) Netbox (inventory management)

Netbox uses a two-phase deployment: 1. Phase 1: Netbox Nomad job starts, database initializes 2. Phase 2: configure_netbox = true triggers null_resource.netbox_inventory to populate inventory

docs.title: VMs and LXC containers (from Terraform)
docs.text: All VMs defined in Layer 1 Terraform (Nomad nodes, Kasm) and LXC containers (Pi-hole nodes) are registered automatically: - VM name, vCPU count, RAM, disk size - IP address with DNS name - Virtual interface (eth0) - Assigned to cluster with site "Home Lab"

docs.title: Proxmox physical nodes
docs.text:
For each Proxmox cluster node, Netbox discovers: - Manufacturer and model (via dmidecode) - CPU model and core count - RAM total - Network interfaces with MAC addresses and detected speed - Storage disks with size and model - Primary IP address

This is gathered by SSH-ing into each Proxmox node from nomad01 during the Terraform apply.

docs.title: Nomad services
docs.text: Service records are created for running Nomad jobs: - Vault (port 8200) - Traefik (ports 80, 443) - Authentik (ports 9000, 9443) - And any other enabled services

docs.title: UniFi network devices (optional)
docs.text: When unifi_address is configured in bootstrap.yml, Netbox also populates: - Switches, access points, gateways from UniFi - Interface details (speed, type, MAC) - Switch port configuration - Network VLANs and prefixes

docs.title: Accessing Netbox
docs.text:
Via DNS (through Traefik): 

https://netbox.<dns-suffix>

Direct access: 

http://<nomad01-ip>:8080

Default credentials: - Username: admin - Password: From Vault: vault kv get -field=admin_password secret/netbox

docs.title: Re-running Inventory Sync
docs.text:
To update Netbox after infrastructure changes, re-apply Layer 2:

./setup.sh --dev
# d5) Deploy services (Traefik, Authentik, secrets)

Or target just the inventory resources:

docker compose run terraform-services apply -auto-approve \
  -target=null_resource.netbox_inventory \
  -target=null_resource.netbox_proxmox_devices \
  -target=null_resource.netbox_unifi_devices

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Netbox secrets are stored in Vault at secret/netbox:

Key Purpose secret_key Netbox application secret key (50 chars, random) postgres_password PostgreSQL database password admin_password Initial admin user password admin_email Admin user email api_token API token used by Terraform to configure Netbox

docs.title: Netbox not accessible
docs.text:
Check the Nomad job status:

ssh labadmin@nomad01 "nomad job status netbox"
ssh labadmin@nomad01 "nomad alloc logs -job netbox"

docs.title: Inventory not populated
docs.text:
The netbox_inventory resource requires configure_netbox = true in terraform/services/terraform.tfvars. This is set automatically when you deploy via option 6 (after Netbox is running).

If you need to force a re-run:

# Remove the Terraform resource state so it re-runs
docker compose run terraform-services state rm null_resource.netbox_inventory
docker compose run terraform-services apply -auto-approve

docs.title: UniFi sync fails
docs.text:
Check the error in the Terraform output. Common issues: - UniFi controller is using a self-signed certificate (SSL errors) - API key is incorrect or expired - Site name is wrong (most setups use "default")

Test the UniFi API manually:

curl -sk -H "X-API-Key: <api-key>" \
  "https://<unifi-ip>/proxy/network/api/s/default/stat/device" | jq '.meta'

docs.title: Pi-hole DNS
docs.text: Pi-hole provides DNS resolution, ad-blocking, and local hostname records for all lab services. It runs as Proxmox LXC containers (one per Proxmox cluster node) and is managed by the lxc-pihole Terraform module.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Property Value Type Proxmox LXC container VMIDs 910, 911, 912 (one per Proxmox node) OS Debian 12 Pi-hole version v6 (FTL engine, TOML config) DNS upstream Unbound (DNS-over-TLS to Cloudflare/Quad9) Replication Gravity Sync (dns-01 is primary) Ports 53 (DNS), 80 (HTTP admin)

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Client DNS query
    |
    v
Pi-hole (ad-block filter, local records)
    |
    |-- local record (*.dns-suffix) --> return IP
    |-- blocked domain              --> return 0.0.0.0
    |-- external query
            v
         Unbound (DNSSEC validation, DNS-over-TLS)
            |
            v
         Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 or Quad9 9.9.9.9 (TLS port 853)

docs.title: DNS Cluster
docs.text:
The number of Pi-hole nodes scales with the Proxmox cluster: - 1 Proxmox node: 1 Pi-hole (dns-01) - 2 Proxmox nodes: 2 Pi-holes (dns-01, dns-02) - 3 Proxmox nodes: 3 Pi-holes (dns-01, dns-02, dns-03)

Nodes are configured in terraform.tfvars under dns_main_nodes:

dns_main_nodes = [
  { hostname = "dns-01", ip = "192.168.1.4/24", gw = "192.168.1.1", target_node = "pve1" },
  { hostname = "dns-02", ip = "192.168.1.5/24", gw = "192.168.1.1", target_node = "pve2" },
  { hostname = "dns-03", ip = "192.168.1.6/24", gw = "192.168.1.1", target_node = "pve3" },
]

docs.title: Gravity Sync
docs.text:
Gravity Sync replicates Pi-hole configuration from the primary (dns-01) to all secondary nodes:

  • Primary: dns-01 (Gravity Sync source)
  • Secondaries: dns-02, dns-03 (sync from primary)
  • Sync interval: 5 minutes (cron job)
  • What replicates: Gravity database, custom DNS records, block lists, allow lists

To force a sync immediately:

ssh labadmin@dns-01 "sudo gravity sync push"
ssh labadmin@dns-02 "sudo gravity sync pull"

docs.title: Pi-hole v6 Configuration
docs.text:
Pi-hole v6 uses a TOML configuration file at /etc/pihole/pihole.toml. The FTL engine replaces the older dnsmasq-based setup.

Pi-hole v6 API change

Pi-hole v6 uses a new REST API at /api/. The old PHP API from Pi-hole v5 is not available. The Terraform ryanwholey/pihole provider is incompatible with v6. DNS records are managed via pihole-FTL --config CLI and SSH null_resource provisioners instead.

Custom local DNS records are stored in the dns.hosts array in pihole.toml and managed by the Layer 2 dns-records.tf Terraform resource.

docs.title: Local DNS Records
docs.text:
Layer 2 Terraform creates all service DNS records in Pi-hole via SSH:

# Records are added using pihole-FTL CLI:
pihole-FTL --config dns.hosts[0]="192.168.1.50 nomad01.mylab.lan"
pihole-FTL --config dns.hosts[1]="192.168.1.50 vault.mylab.lan"
# ...etc

To rebuild all DNS records without a full redeploy:

./setup.sh --dev
# d11) Rebuild DNS records

docs.title: Unbound Configuration
docs.text:
Each Pi-hole node runs Unbound as a DNS resolver for external queries. Unbound configuration is stored in the lxc-pihole module at terraform/lxc-pihole/files/unbound.conf.

Key settings: - DNS-over-TLS: Queries forwarded to Cloudflare (1.1.1.1@853) and Quad9 (9.9.9.9@853) over TLS - DNSSEC: Enabled for validation - Prefetching: Enabled to reduce latency on popular domains

docs.title: High Availability
docs.text:
When ha_dns_enabled: true is configured in bootstrap.yml, keepalived VRRP provides a Virtual IP (VIP) that floats between Pi-hole nodes:

<dns-ha-vip>  --> dns-01 (priority 101, MASTER)
               if dns-01 fails --> dns-02 (priority 100)
               if dns-02 fails --> dns-03 (priority 99)

Clients configure only the VIP as their DNS server. Failover is automatic when the master Pi-hole's DNS check fails.

Required: ha_dns_vrrp_router_id must not conflict with any other VRRP on your network. Requires privileged = true on the LXC containers (for NET_ADMIN capability).

docs.title: Accessing Pi-hole Admin
docs.text:
Via DNS (through Traefik): 

https://pihole.<dns-suffix>

Direct access: 

http://<dns-01-ip>/admin

Authentik forward auth

Pi-hole is protected by Authentik forward auth when accessed through Traefik. Direct access via IP bypasses authentication.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Pi-hole admin and root passwords are randomly generated by Terraform and stored in Vault at secret/pihole:

# View the Pi-hole admin password
vault kv get -field=admin_password secret/pihole

docs.title: DNS not resolving after deployment
docs.text:
1. Check that your client is using the Pi-hole IP (or HA VIP) as its DNS server
  2. Test DNS resolution directly from Pi-hole: dig @<dns-01-ip> google.com
  3. Check Pi-hole FTL status: ssh labadmin@dns-01 "systemctl status pihole-FTL"
  4. View FTL logs: ssh labadmin@dns-01 "journalctl -u pihole-FTL -f"

docs.title: Local hostnames not resolving
docs.text:
1. Check DNS records exist in Pi-hole: Browse to /admin/dns-records
  2. Force rebuild: ./setup.sh --dev then d11) Rebuild DNS records
  3. Verify the record: dig @<dns-01-ip> vault.<dns-suffix>

docs.title: Gravity Sync not working
docs.text:
1. Check SSH connectivity between nodes: 
    ssh labadmin@dns-01 "ssh -i /etc/gravity-sync/gravity-sync.rsa dns-02 echo ok"
  2. Run manual sync: ssh labadmin@dns-01 "sudo gravity sync push"
  3. Check sync logs: ssh labadmin@dns-01 "sudo gravity sync logs"

docs.title: Container provisioning fails during apt-get
docs.text:
The bootstrap_dns setting controls which DNS server LXC containers use during provisioning. If your network blocks external DNS (1.1.1.1, etc.), set bootstrap_dns to your gateway IP:

# terraform/terraform.tfvars
bootstrap_dns = "<gateway-ip>"

This is auto-populated from the network.gateway in bootstrap.yml during bootstrap.

docs.title: Samba AD
docs.text: Samba AD provides Active Directory Domain Services for the lab environment. It deploys two domain controllers — DC01 as the primary (provisioning a new domain) and DC02 as a replica — across separate Nomad nodes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Property Value Nomad Job samba-ad Image nowsci/samba-domain:latest Type service (2 task groups) DC01 Node Pinned to nomad01 DC02 Node Pinned to nomad02 Vault Role samba-ad (WIF) Privileged Yes Storage /srv/gluster/nomad-data/samba-dc01/, samba-dc02/ Ports 88 (Kerberos), 389 (LDAP), 636 (LDAPS), 445 (SMB)

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Select option 4 from the setup menu:

./setup.sh
# 4) Samba AD + LDAP Account Manager

This deploys: 1. Samba AD domain controllers 2. LDAP Account Manager (LAM) for web-based user management 3. Service accounts (domain-join-svc, authentik-sync, lam-admin) 4. DNS forwarding rules in Pi-hole for the AD realm

The deployment script:

  1. Prompts for the AD realm (derived from dns_postfix, e.g., AD.MYLAB.LAN)
  2. Stores the admin password in Vault at secret/data/samba-ad
  3. Configures Pi-hole DNS forwarding for the AD realm
  4. Submits the Nomad job with variable substitution
  5. Deploys DC01 first, then DC02 (if nomad02 exists)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before deploying Samba AD, the following must be in place:

  1. Nomad cluster -- At least nomad01 operational (nomad02 for DC02)
  2. Vault -- Running and initialized with the samba-dc role configured (menu option 8)
  3. Vault secrets -- Admin password stored at secret/data/samba-ad:
    • admin_password -- Domain administrator password
  4. Pi-hole DNS -- Running and configured for AD realm forwarding
  5. Local storage -- /opt/samba-dc01/ on nomad01 and /opt/samba-dc02/ on nomad02

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph nomad01["nomad01"]
        DC1[Samba DC01<br/>JOIN=false<br/>Primary DC]
        DC1_DNS[DNS :5353]
        DC1_KRB[Kerberos :88]
        DC1_LDAP[LDAP :389]
        DC1_SMB[SMB :445]
    end

    subgraph nomad02["nomad02"]
        DC2[Samba DC02<br/>JOIN=true<br/>Replica DC]
        DC2_DNS[DNS :5354]
        DC2_KRB[Kerberos :88]
        DC2_LDAP[LDAP :389]
        DC2_SMB[SMB :445]
    end

    subgraph pihole["Pi-hole DNS"]
        FWD[AD Realm Forwarding<br/>*.ad.mylab.lan]
    end

    subgraph vault["Vault"]

    DC2 -->|DNSFORWARDER| DC1

    FWD -->|port 5353| DC1
    FWD -->|port 5354| DC2

    DC1 -->|WIF JWT| vault

docs.title: Domain Controller Groups
docs.text: The Nomad job defines two separate groups -- dc01 and dc02 -- each pinned to a different Nomad node. This separation ensures the domain controllers run on different physical hosts for redundancy.

docs.title: DC01 -- Primary Domain Controller
docs.text:
DC01 provisions a new Active Directory domain. It runs with JOIN=false, meaning it creates the domain from scratch on first start.

Property Value Node nomad01 Role Primary (provisions domain) JOIN false DNS Port 5353 Storage /opt/samba-dc01/samba and /opt/samba-dc01/krb5

docs.title: Ports (DC01)
docs.text: Port Protocol Service 5353 TCP/UDP DNS (non-standard to avoid Pi-hole conflict on 53) 88 TCP/UDP Kerberos 389 TCP LDAP 636 TCP LDAP over TLS 445 TCP SMB 3268 TCP Global Catalog 3269 TCP Global Catalog over TLS

docs.title: DC02 -- Replica Domain Controller
docs.text:
DC02 joins the existing domain as a replica. It runs with JOIN=true and uses DC01 as its DNS forwarder.

Property Value Node nomad02 Role Replica (joins domain) JOIN true JOINSITE Default-First-Site-Name DNSFORWARDER nomad01 IP DNS Port 5354 Storage /opt/samba-dc02/samba and /opt/samba-dc02/krb5

docs.title: Ports (DC02)
docs.text:
DC02 uses the same ports as DC01 except for DNS:

Port Protocol Service 5354 TCP/UDP DNS (different from DC01 to allow Pi-hole forwarding to both) 88 TCP/UDP Kerberos 389 TCP LDAP 636 TCP LDAP over TLS 445 TCP SMB 3268 TCP Global Catalog 3269 TCP Global Catalog over TLS

docs.title: Single-Node Support
docs.text: If the Nomad cluster has only one or two nodes and nomad02 does not exist, the deployment script automatically skips DC02. Only DC01 is deployed, providing a fully functional single-DC domain without replication.

docs.title: Local Storage Requirement
docs.text:
POSIX ACL Requirement

Samba AD requires POSIX ACL support on its data directory. GlusterFS FUSE mounts do not provide this, so Samba DCs use local storage instead of GlusterFS.

Each DC stores its data on the local filesystem of its Nomad node:

DC Samba Data Kerberos Config DC01 /opt/samba-dc01/samba:/var/lib/samba /opt/samba-dc01/krb5:/etc/krb5 DC02 /opt/samba-dc02/samba:/var/lib/samba /opt/samba-dc02/krb5:/etc/krb5

Because storage is local (not replicated via GlusterFS), each DC maintains its own copy of the AD database. Active Directory's built-in replication protocol keeps them synchronized.

docs.title: Vault Secrets Integration
docs.text:
Samba AD uses Vault WIF to retrieve the domain administrator password at startup:

vault {
  role        = "samba-dc"
  change_mode = "noop"
}
  • role = "samba-dc" -- Maps to the samba-dc Vault policy which grants read access to secret/data/samba-ad.
  • change_mode = "noop" -- Secrets changes do not restart the container. Active Directory is stateful and restarting a DC can cause replication issues. Password changes must be handled manually.

docs.title: Secrets Template
docs.text:
template {
  data = <<EOH
{{ with secret "secret/data/samba-ad" }}
DOMAINPASS={{ .Data.data.admin_password }}
{{ end }}
DOMAIN=<ad_realm>
HOSTIP=<node_ip>
DNSFORWARDER=<forwarder_ip>
JOIN=false
INSECURELDAP=true
NOCOMPLEXITY=true
EOH
  destination = "secrets/samba.env"
  env         = true
}
Variable DC01 Value DC02 Value DOMAINPASS From Vault From Vault DOMAIN AD realm (e.g., AD.MYLAB.LAN) Same HOSTIP nomad01 IP nomad02 IP DNSFORWARDER Pi-hole IP nomad01 IP JOIN false true JOINSITE (not set) Default-First-Site-Name INSECURELDAP true true NOCOMPLEXITY true true

docs.title: DNS Forwarding
docs.text: Pi-hole is configured to forward queries for the AD realm to the Samba DCs. This allows clients using Pi-hole as their DNS server to resolve AD hostnames without additional configuration.

docs.title: Forwarding Rules
docs.text:
Query Pattern Forwarded To Port *.ad.<dns_postfix> nomad01 (DC01) 5353 *.ad.<dns_postfix> nomad02 (DC02) 5354

The setup script configures this automatically in Pi-hole's dnsmasq configuration.

docs.title: DNS Records
docs.text:
The deployment also creates DNS records in Pi-hole:

Record Points To samba-dc01.ad.<dns_postfix> nomad01 IP samba-dc02.ad.<dns_postfix> nomad02 IP

docs.title: Why Non-Standard DNS Ports?
docs.text:
Samba AD runs its own DNS server internally, but Pi-hole already occupies port 53 on the network. To resolve this:

  • DC01 uses port 5353 for DNS
  • DC02 uses port 5354 for DNS
  • Pi-hole forwards AD realm queries to these non-standard ports
  • Clients never need to know about the port mapping -- they query Pi-hole on port 53 as usual

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
Each DC registers two services with Nomad, each with a TCP health check:

Service Port Check Type Interval samba-dc01 / samba-dc02 LDAP (389) TCP 30s samba-dc01-kerberos / samba-dc02-kerberos Kerberos (88) TCP 30s

Both checks use a 5-second timeout. If LDAP or Kerberos becomes unreachable, Nomad marks the service as unhealthy.

docs.title: Domain Configuration
docs.text:
The AD realm and NetBIOS domain name are derived from the lab's dns_postfix:

Setting Example (dns_postfix = mylab.lan) AD Realm AD.MYLAB.LAN NetBIOS Domain AD Domain DN DC=ad,DC=mylab,DC=lan Admin User Administrator

NetBIOS Name Limit

The NetBIOS domain name has a 15-character maximum. The deployment script uses the first component of the AD realm (e.g., AD), which stays well within this limit.

docs.title: Service Tags
docs.text:
Each DC is tagged with metadata for service discovery:

# DC01
tags = [
  "dc=primary",
  "realm=AD.MYLAB.LAN",
]

# DC02
tags = [
  "dc=replica",
  "realm=AD.MYLAB.LAN",
]

docs.title: Verifying the Deployment
docs.text:
After deploying Samba AD, verify both DCs are running:

# Check job status (both dc01 and dc02 groups)
docker compose run --rm nomad job status samba-dc

# Verify services are registered
docker compose run --rm nomad service list

# Test LDAP connectivity to DC01
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://nomad01:389 -b "dc=ad,dc=mylab,dc=lan" -s base

# Test Kerberos on DC01
ssh nomad01 'docker exec $(docker ps -qf name=samba-dc) samba-tool domain info 127.0.0.1'

# Check AD replication status (run from DC01)
ssh nomad01 'docker exec $(docker ps -qf name=samba-dc) samba-tool drs showrepl'

# List domain users
ssh nomad01 'docker exec $(docker ps -qf name=samba-dc) samba-tool user list'

# Check allocation logs
docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job samba-dc

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
DC won't start

The domain controller fails to start or crashes on launch.

  1. Check container logs: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job samba-dc
  2. Verify the storage directories exist and have correct permissions: 
    ssh nomad01 'ls -la /opt/samba-dc01/'
ssh nomad02 'ls -la /opt/samba-dc02/'
  3. Check that ports are not already in use: 
    ssh nomad01 'sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ":88|:389|:445"'
  4. Verify Vault secrets are accessible: 
    export VAULT_ADDR="http://nomad01:8200"
vault kv get secret/samba-ad
  5. For a fresh start, stop the job and clean the data directory: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad job stop -purge samba-dc
ssh nomad01 'sudo rm -rf /opt/samba-dc01/*'
AD replication failing between DC01 and DC02

The domain controllers are not synchronizing.

  1. Check replication status from inside DC01: 
    ssh nomad01 'docker exec $(docker ps -qf name=samba-dc) samba-tool drs showrepl'
  2. Verify DC02 can reach DC01 over the network: 
    ssh nomad02 'nc -zv nomad01 389'
ssh nomad02 'nc -zv nomad01 88'
  3. Check that DNS is resolving correctly: 
    ssh nomad02 'nslookup samba-dc01.ad.mylab.lan'
  4. Inspect DC02 logs for join/replication errors: 
    docker compose run --rm nomad alloc logs -job samba-dc
Domain join from a client machine fails

A workstation or server cannot join the AD domain.

  1. Verify DNS forwards the AD realm to the Samba DCs. Test from the client: 
    nslookup ad.mylab.lan
nslookup _ldap._tcp.ad.mylab.lan
  2. Check Pi-hole's AD forwarding configuration: 
    ssh dns-01 'cat /etc/dnsmasq.d/10-ad-forward.conf'
  3. Test LDAP connectivity from the client: 
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://nomad01:389 -b "dc=ad,dc=mylab,dc=lan" -s base
  4. Verify the domain admin credentials: 
    export VAULT_ADDR="http://nomad01:8200"
vault kv get -field=admin_password secret/samba-ad
LDAP connection fails

LDAP queries return errors or timeouts.

  1. Test basic TCP connectivity: 
    nc -zv nomad01 389
  2. Test LDAP bind: 
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://nomad01:389 \
  -D "Administrator@ad.mylab.lan" \
  -w "<admin_password>" \
  -b "dc=ad,dc=mylab,dc=lan" \
  "(objectClass=user)"
  3. Check that INSECURELDAP=true is set (allows unencrypted LDAP binds).
  4. If using LDAPs (port 636), verify the DC has a valid TLS certificate.
Kerberos authentication errors

Clients receive Kerberos errors when authenticating.

  1. Verify the Kerberos service is running: 
    ssh nomad01 'nc -zv 127.0.0.1 88'
  2. Check time synchronization -- Kerberos requires clocks to be within 5 minutes: 
    ssh nomad01 'date'
ssh nomad02 'date'
  3. Verify the realm is correct in the client's krb5.conf: 
    [libdefaults]
    default_realm = AD.MYLAB.LAN

[realms]
    AD.MYLAB.LAN = {
        kdc = nomad01
        admin_server = nomad01
    }
